newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Jill Sobule, an accidental heroine for gays.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Jill Sobule, an accidental heroine for gays.

text.p: Jill Sobule had almost given up her dreams of pop stardom when she got a second shot at the big time thanks to a record in which she declared "I Kissed a Girl."
She has gone from waiting tables and selling shoes to becoming a heroine for lesbians.
Seven years ago Sobule got her first chance at fame recording a folk music album called "Things Here Are Different" with producer Todd Rundgren for MCA.

"Other than (a few) Todd Rundgren fans I don't think there was anyone who bought that record," Sobule said in a recent interview with Reuters. The second album, recorded with celebrated English performer Joe Jackson and guests "Wendy & Lisa" from Prince's band, never saw the light of day after Sobule was dumped by her recording company.
Her career as a musician seemingly over, Sobule went back to work in a series of odd jobs including a brief stint waiting tables, selling shoes in New York and working with a wedding photographer.

"The problem was I didn't really have any marketable skills to do anything else," she said. "A few years later, after being dropped by my label, I thought 'I hate this music business, this is not fun,' but I didn't know what else to do with my life so I kept on writing."
SIGNED IN A FLUKE
Eventually she was signed by Atlantic Records "almost like a fluke" in 1994 when a lawyer she was friendly with played a rough tape of her songs to an Atlantic talent scout.
"And they called me that night and asked me to come down to the office, and I did, and I got signed," she said.
Her first self-titled album with Atlantic spawned the hit single "I Kissed A Girl" that brought fame and controversy.
Some radio stations would only play the song late in the evening while one station in Nashville aired a "get the kids out of the room" public service announcement before playing the song.

"It was a double-edged sword because with all the artists out there at least it was something that got me noticed ... but on the other hand it was the only thing that people knew me for and there is a lot more," she said.
"I would look on the Internet and I'd see things like 'Love it,' or 'Why doesn't she come out of the closet?' or 'She's a fake lesbian.'"

The song, which Sobule claims was the first ever top 40 hit about a lesbian kiss, became a favourite on MTV where her tongue-in-cheek video starring beefcake male model Fabio was regularly played. Solbule was even honoured by the Gay and Lesbian Alliance even though she does not consider herself gay.
"I've travelled but I would not say I'm gay. I suppose if someone had to use a label ... I've had a bisexual life."
Despite all the attention on her sexual preferences Sobule is happy the song was released as a single.
"The good thing about it is there was a lot of people who came up to me and said they wished there was a song like that when they were young," she said.
NEW ALBUM
Sobule is back on the road promoting a new album "Happy Town" which again uses happy-go-lucky melodies to diguise a darker lyrical content.

"I always try and write things that poeple don't write about in pop or rock music and deal with real subjects," Sobule said about her songs. "There is something more ironic, and almost sick, about having a happy little melody and having a lyric that doesn't quite fit."

Among the topics Sobule tackles on her latest album is her biological clock which still is not going off ("Barren Egg") and the hypocrisy of the religous right ("Soldiers of Christ"). Anti-depressants, something Sobule knows about from her 20s when she was battling with eating disorders and depression, is the topic of the title track "Happy Town."

"I was in a real funk and they helped me but ... one bad side effect, especially for women but for men too, was it really takes your sexual desires right down and a lot of people become inorgasmic," she said. "Maybe I'd rather be more depressed."

Life on the road can be hard, Sobule said, and sometimes generating sales for the record company makes her feel like a "unit whore." "This is not a very easy industry to be in ... and I'm still poor." But all told Sobule prefers life as an up-and-coming rock star to her previous jobs.
Later Sobule won over the crowd at the Caprice supper club in Redondo Beach and jokingly pleaded with the audience, "Please buy my record, don't send me back to Barney's!"
